text:
The passage repays attention to what it withholds. Sarah is nowhere in Genesis 22, and in the verse immediately following the chapter her death is announced, Genesis 23:1; the scene implies, though it will not say, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants, Genesis 22:19; Isaac is not named in that return. At the point where a lesser story would linger, this narration turns aside. Its silence is not mere absence; it gives evidence.

Against this it may be urged that the chapter observes only the economy of ancient narrative, which seldom records feeling and never explains. This may, perhaps, in some sense, be true. Yet the same narrator elsewhere gives feeling plainly enough: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The withholding here is chosen. The writer knows the value of what is withheld; and Restraint, in this voice, becomes a form of accusation.
